lessons.title: Grace, the foundation of everything
lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 1: Grace, the foundation of everything**

Before anything about being a better man, the Bible starts with what God has already done. Ephesians 2:8–9 (NIV) says, "For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God—not by works, so that no one can boast." Grace means God gives us what we could never earn. You don't become a better husband and father to win God's love; you grow because you already have it.

John 3:16 (NIV) shows where that grace comes from: "For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life." Billy Graham built his whole ministry on this message, and his book *Peace with God* explains it in plain language. When you're ready for the man, husband, and father part, Tony Evans' *Kingdom Man* is written exactly for that.

**To reflect on this week:** Read Ephesians 2:1–10 in the NLT, which is very easy to follow. Then ask yourself one question: do I ever act like I have to earn God's approval, or my family's?

**Ephesians 2:1–10 (NLT)**

¹ Once you were dead because of your disobedience and your many sins. ² You used to live in sin, just like the rest of the world, obeying the devil—the commander of the powers in the unseen world. He is the spirit at work in the hearts of those who refuse to obey God. ³ All of us used to live that way, following the passionate desires and inclinations of our sinful nature. By our very nature we were subject to God's anger, just like everyone else.

⁴ But God is so rich in mercy, and he loved us so much, ⁵ that even though we were dead because of our sins, he gave us life when he raised Christ from the dead. (It is only by God's grace that you have been saved!) ⁶ For he raised us from the dead along with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly realms because we are united with Christ Jesus. ⁷ So God can point to us in all future ages as examples of the incredible wealth of his grace and kindness toward us, as shown in all he has done for us who are united with Christ Jesus.

⁸ God saved you by his grace when you believed. And you can't take credit for this; it is a gift from God. ⁹ Salvation is not a reward for the good things we have done, so none of us can boast about it. ¹⁰ For we are God's masterpiece. He has created us anew in Christ Jesus, so we can do the good things he planned for us long ago.

*Holy Bible, New Living Translation, © 1996, 2004, 2015 by Tyndale House Foundation. Used by permission. All rights reserved.*

Look at the order: verses 1–9 are what God did, and only then does verse 10 talk about the good things we do. The good things you do as a husband and father flow out of grace. They don't earn it. From now on I'll include the full reading in every lesson.

**Lesson 2: Who God Is**

Good morning, Gregory. Yesterday's lesson was about grace, which is God saving us as a gift we didn't earn. Today we look at the God who gives that grace. How you picture God shapes everything else: how you pray, how you deal with failure, and even how you lead at home.

In Psalm 103, David reminds himself what God is really like. God isn't a harsh judge waiting for us to slip up. He forgives, heals, redeems, and fills our lives with good things. Verse 8 echoes what God told Moses about himself in Exodus 34. He is compassionate and merciful, slow to get angry, and full of unfailing love. When we turn to him, our sins aren't just set aside. They're removed "as far from us as the east is from the west."

Verse 13 matters a lot for you as a dad. "The Lord is like a father to his children." Your children's first picture of fatherhood is you. God is the perfect Father, and the more you get to know his tenderness and patience, the more you'll have to give your family. If you'd like to go deeper, J.I. Packer's classic book *Knowing God* is a great next step.

**Today's reading: Psalm 103:1–13 (NLT)**

*A psalm of David.*
¹ Let all that I am praise the Lord; with my whole heart, I will praise his holy name.
² Let all that I am praise the Lord; may I never forget the good things he does for me.
³ He forgives all my sins and heals all my diseases.
⁴ He redeems me from death and crowns me with love and tender mercies.
⁵ He fills my life with good things. My youth is renewed like the eagle's!
⁶ The Lord gives righteousness and justice to all who are treated unfairly.
⁷ He revealed his character to Moses and his deeds to the people of Israel.
⁸ The Lord is compassionate and merciful, slow to get angry and filled with unfailing love.
⁹ He will not constantly accuse us, nor remain angry forever.
¹⁰ He does not punish us for all our sins; he does not deal harshly with us, as we deserve.
¹¹ For his unfailing love toward those who fear him is as great as the height of the heavens above the earth.
¹² He has removed our sins as far from us as the east is from the west.
¹³ The Lord is like a father to his children, tender and compassionate to those who fear him.

*Scripture quotations are taken from the Holy Bible, New Living Translation, copyright © 1996, 2004, 2015 by Tyndale House Foundation. Used by permission of Tyndale House Publishers, Carol Stream, Illinois 60188. All rights reserved.*

**Reflection:** Verse 8 says God is "slow to get angry and filled with unfailing love." Think of one moment this week with your wife or kids when you could show that same patience. What would it look like for you to be slow to anger there?

**Lesson 3: Who Jesus Is**

Yesterday we saw God as a compassionate Father. Today's question is the one everything else depends on: who is Jesus? Paul answers it in one of the richest passages in the Bible. Jesus isn't just a good teacher or a moral example. He is "the image of the invisible God," so if you want to know what the Father is like, you look at Jesus.

Paul makes three big claims. First, Jesus is over creation: everything was made through him and for him, and he's the one holding it all together right now, even on the days when your life feels like it's coming apart. Second, he's over the church. He's its head, and he's the first to rise from the dead for good, the promise that his people will rise too. Third, he's the peacemaker. The fullness of God lives in him, and he brought us back to God "by making peace through his blood, shed on the cross." Lesson 1's grace has a name and a face, and it's Jesus.

For a man, a husband, and a father, this matters in a practical way. Jesus isn't one more thing to fit into your schedule. He's the center everything else holds onto. When he has "the supremacy" in your life, your marriage, your work, and your parenting get steadier, because they're no longer carrying weight only he can carry.

**Today's reading: Colossians 1:15–20 (NIV)**

*The Supremacy of the Son of God*
15 The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. 16 For in him all things were created: things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or powers or rulers or authorities; all things have been created through him and for him. 17 He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. 18 And he is the head of the body, the church; he is the beginning and the firstborn from among the dead, so that in everything he might have the supremacy. 19 For God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him, 20 and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether things on earth or things in hea...n of all creation," and the LSB keeps that word for word. The NIV puts the meaning into the wording. In the Bible, "firstborn" often means the one with the highest rank and the right to inherit, the way God calls David his "firstborn" in Psalm 89:27 even though David was the youngest son. Verse 16 settles it: all things were created in him, so he isn't part of creation. He's its Lord.

*Verse 19.* The NIV says "God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him," and the LSB says "in Him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell." The Greek is short and a little open here. The LSB stays close to that form, while the NIV makes it plain that God is the one who was pleased. Both say the same thing: everything God is lives fully in Jesus.

**Going deeper**

- John Piper's book *Seeing and Savoring Jesus Christ* is a short, readable look at who Jesus is.
- Billy Graham's *Peace with God* is a classic on how Jesus makes peace between us and God.
- Grace Life is preaching through Hebrews in its "What a Savior" series, and Hebrews is also about Jesus being greater than everything else. Yesterday's sermon, [What a Savior, Part 11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sp9u-I5s3dk), fits right alongside today's reading, and the rest of the series is on their [media page](https://yourgracelife.com/media).

**Reflection question**

Verse 17 says "in him all things hold together." What are you trying to hold together on your own right now, at home, at work, or in your marriage, that you need to hand back to Jesus this week? What would it look like to show Sanqueta and the kids that he's at the center?

lessons.title: Sin and Forgiveness, Walking in the Light
lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 4: Sin and Forgiveness, Walking in the Light**

Good morning, Gregory. Yesterday we looked at who Jesus is. Today is about what He does for us when we fail. John starts with a simple fact: God is light, with no darkness in Him at all. If we're honest, that's a problem for us, because all of us have some darkness in us. John names two ways we try to get around it. We can say "I'm fine, I don't really sin" (v. 8, 10), or we can claim to be close to God while quietly living in the dark (v. 6). Both are lies, and they keep us stuck.

God's way out is confession (v. 9). To confess means to agree with God about what we did, calling it what He calls it instead of making excuses. The promise is that He is "faithful and just" to forgive. That's not because God goes easy on sin. It's because Jesus already paid for it. That's why 2:1–2 calls Jesus our advocate, the one who stands up for us with the Father, and the sacrifice for our sins. Forgiveness rests on the cross, not on how sorry we feel.

This matters at home too. Walking in the light gives us "fellowship with one another" (v. 7). A husband and father who's quick to admit his wrongs, first to God and then to his wife and kids, shows them what grace looks like. If you want to go deeper, John Piper's short book *Fifty Reasons Why Jesus Came to Die* is good here (its first reason is "To absorb the wrath of God"), and so is Billy Graham's classic *Peace with God*, which covers sin and forgiveness in plain words.

**Today's reading: 1 John 1:5–2:2 (NIV)**

5 This is the message we have heard from him and declare to you: God is light; in him there is no darkness at all. 6 If we claim to have fellowship with him and yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not live out the truth. 7 But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, purifies us from all sin. 8 If we claim to be without sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. 9 If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness. 10 If we claim we have not sinned, we make him out to be a liar and his word is not in us.

2:1 My dear children, I write this to you so that you will not sin. But if anybody does sin, we have an advocate with the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. 2 He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.

**Translation note (1 John 2:2)**
NIV: "He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins"
LSB: "He Himself is the propitiation for our sins"
The Greek word here is *hilasmos*. The LSB translates word for word and keeps the older theological term "propitiation," which means a sacrifice that turns away God's righteous anger against sin and makes Him favorable toward us. The NIV translates by meaning and uses "atoning sacrifice," which is easier to read but doesn't spell out the idea of God's wrath being satisfied. Both are faithful. The LSB just makes it clearer that on the cross Jesus took the judgment we deserved, which is the point Piper stresses in the book above.

**Reflection question:** Is there something you've been quietly keeping in the dark, whether with God, with Sanqueta, or with one of the kids, that you could bring into the light this week by simply saying "I was wrong, please forgive me"?

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 5: Faith and Repentance, Coming Home to the Father**

Yesterday we saw that when we confess our sins, Jesus is our advocate. Today is about the turn that starts it all. Repentance means more than feeling bad. It means changing your mind about your sin and turning around, away from it and back toward God. Faith is the other half of that same turn: trusting that God will really receive you because of Jesus, not because you've cleaned yourself up first.

Jesus paints this in the story of the lost son. The younger son wanted the father's stuff without the father. When everything ran out, he "came to his senses." That's repentance: he saw his life truthfully, admitted "I have sinned," and got up and went home. Faith is what moved his feet. He believed his father was good enough to go back to, even if all he hoped for was a servant's job.

Look at the father, though. He sees his son "while he was still a long way off," runs to him, and covers him with a robe, a ring, and a feast before the son even finishes his speech. That's the heart of God toward anyone who turns back. For you as a dad, it's also a picture of the kind of father you get to be: one who watches the road, runs toward his kids, and restores them instead of making them earn their way back.

For further reading, Billy Graham's *Peace with God* walks through repentance and faith in plain language, and [Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org), John Piper's ministry, has many articles and sermons on repentance.

**Today's reading: Luke 15:11–24 (NIV)**

11 Jesus continued: "There was a man who had two sons. 12 The younger one said to his father, 'Father, give me my share of the estate.' So he divided his property between them.

13 "Not long after that, the younger son got together all he had, set off for a distant country and there squandered his wealth in wild living. 14 After he had spent everything, there was a severe famine in that whole country, and he began to be in need. 15 So he went and hi...up and went to his father.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him.

21 "The son said to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.'

22 "But the father said to his servants, 'Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. 23 Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate. 24 For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.' So they began to celebrate."

**Translation note**

*Verse 17.* The NIV says "When he came to his senses," and the LSB says "But when he came to himself." The Greek literally reads "coming to himself." The LSB keeps that word-for-word wording, which suggests that sin had made him a stranger to who he really was. The NIV gives the meaning in everyday English: he finally started thinking clearly.

*Verse 22.* The NIV says "the father said to his servants," and the LSB says "the father said to his slaves." The Greek word *doulos* can mean either one. The LSB translates it more literally. The contrast it draws is striking: the son asked to be treated like a hired man, and the father gives orders to his household slaves to dress him as an honored son.

**Reflection question:** Is there an area of your life where you need to "come to your senses" and turn back to God today? And when one of your kids, or Sanqueta, comes to you after messing up, do they meet a father and husband who runs toward them?

**Lesson 6: The Holy Spirit, the Helper Who Stays With You**

After Jesus, the next person of God you need to know is the Holy Spirit. On the night before the cross, Jesus told his friends he was leaving, and that he would not leave them alone. He would ask the Father to send "another advocate," the Spirit of truth, to be with them forever and to live in them. You are not an orphan in the Christian life. The same Spirit who was with the disciples is with you and in you.

Tony Evans teaches that the Greek word *parakletos* means someone called alongside: a helper, an advocate, a companion of the same kind as Jesus. The Spirit walks with you and lives in you at the same time, so you are never by yourself. John Piper, in *The Holy Spirit: He Is God!* (on John 14:15–17, 25–26), stresses that the Spirit is a person, not a force, and fully God, your Teacher and Counselor. Billy Graham likewise describes him as the personal Helper who lives in believers, helps us grasp Scripture, and gives us power to live for Christ.

Your church has already preached this passage. Pastor Joel's sermon [We Believe in the Holy Spirit](https://web.sermonaudio.com/sermons/762508482639) (Grace Life Baptist Church, June 29, 2025) walks through John 14–16. He shows that the Spirit fully lives in every believer from the moment they're saved, and that he helps and advocates, teaches and reminds, points to Jesus, convicts, guides through the Word, and glorifies Christ. It's not fog machines or vibes. It's the living God at work through Scripture.

**Today's reading: John 14:15–26 (NIV)**

15 "If you love me, keep my commands. 16 And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another advocate to help you and be with you forever— 17 the Spirit of truth. The world cannot accept him, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you know him, for he lives with you and will be in you. 18 I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you. 19 Before long, the world will not see me anymore, but you w... you. 21 Whoever has my commands and keeps them is the one who loves me. The one who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I too will love them and show myself to them."

22 Then Judas (not Judas Iscariot) said, "But, Lord, why do you intend to show yourself to us and not to the world?"

23 Jesus replied, "Anyone who loves me will obey my teaching. My Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them. 24 Anyone who does not love me will not obey my teaching. These words you hear are not my own; they belong to the Father who sent me.

25 "All this I have spoken while still with you. 26 But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have said to you."

**Translation note**

*Verse 15.* The NIV says "If you love me, *keep* my commands," and the LSB says "If you love Me, *you will keep* My commandments." The LSB stays closer to the Greek future tense, which shows that obedience naturally grows out of love. The NIV's "keep" can read like a command. Both point to the same link: real love for Jesus shows up in a life that follows him.

*Verses 16 and 26.* Both the NIV and the LSB say "advocate." The LSB's footnote gives the Greek word, *parakletos*, which means one called alongside as a helper. It's a rich word, and English translations bring out different sides of it: legal advocate, counselor, and helper.

**Reflection question:** Where do you feel most alone as a husband or dad this week, and how does it change things to remember the Spirit is already with you and in you there?

**Lesson 7: Prayer, Talking With Your Father**

Yesterday we sat with the Holy Spirit, the Helper who stays with you. Today Jesus shows you what to do with that: talk to your Father. Prayer isn't a performance or a pile of fancy words. It's a son coming to his Dad.

Jesus warns against praying to be seen and against empty repetition. Then he gives a pattern, not a script to mumble. Billy Graham put it plainly: the Lord's Prayer is a model, but "simply saying a memorized prayer doesn't accomplish anything if we aren't paying attention to its meaning and saying it from our hearts." Tony Evans teaches the same shape as a pattern for real conversation with God: worship, God's will, daily needs, forgiveness, and protection. John Piper presses that the opening lines are petitions too. "Hallowed be your name," "Your kingdom come," and "Your will be done" are requests that God's name be cherished first in your heart, then in your home and beyond. As a husband and dad, that means your closet prayer shapes how you lead Sanqueta and the kids, seeking God's name and will before you ask for bread.

At Grace Life, Joel Frederick's [Acts: Church On The Move Part 18](https://yourgracelife.com/media/acts-church-on-the-move-part-18) (Acts 12:1–25) is tagged for prayer and trust, the church praying while God acts. Worth a listen when you want to see prayer lived out in the early church.

**Today's reading: Matthew 6:5–13 (NIV)**

"And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by others. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward in full. But when you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen. Then your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. And when you pray, do not keep on babbling like pagans, for they think they will be heard because of their many words. Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

"This, then, is how you should pray:

"'Our Father in heaven,
hallowed be your name,
your kingdom come,
your will be done,
on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
And forgive us our debts,
as we also have forgiven our debtors.
And lead us not into temptation,
but deliver us from the evil one.'"

**Translation note**

*Verse 7.* The NIV says "do not keep on babbling like pagans," and the LSB says "do not use meaningless repetition as the Gentiles do." Same warning: empty volume doesn't impress God. The LSB stays closer to the Greek idea of vain, empty phrases, and the NIV's "babbling" captures the sense in everyday English.

*Verse 6.* The NIV says "go into your room… your Father, who is unseen," and the LSB says "go into your inner room… your Father who is in secret." The LSB's word-for-word feel stresses a private inner place and a Father who meets you there. The NIV's meaning-based "unseen" says the same thing more simply.

*Verse 13.* The LSB brackets "[For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.]" and notes that early manuscripts omit it. The NIV puts a similar note in a footnote. Many churches still pray that closing praise; the earliest copies of Matthew often end at "the evil one."

**Reflection question:** Where can you take ten quiet minutes today, before the kids are up or after they're down, to pray this pattern from the heart for Sanqueta, Jordyn, Elijah, and Enoch: God's name first, then his will in your home, then today's needs, forgiveness, and protection?

**Lesson 8: Reading Scripture — God-breathed words that equip you**

Prayer (yesterday) is talking with your Father. Reading Scripture is listening to Him. Paul writes to Timothy like a spiritual son: stay in what you learned, because the writings themselves are *God-breathed*. Not merely inspiring ideas, but God’s own words on the page—able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and to shape you for every good work as a man, husband, and father.

John Piper puts it plainly in *[All Scripture Is Breathed Out by God — Continue in It](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/all-scripture-is-breathed-out-by-god-continue-in-it)*: the focus is on the *writings*, so that when you open the Bible you are hearing God. Scripture teaches, then reproves (stops you), corrects (turns you), and trains you in righteousness—so you are thoroughly equipped. A short daily reading gives you regular opportunities to understand and practice what God says; longer study can deepen that habit too.

Open [Grace Life’s sermon media](https://yourgracelife.com/media) anytime you want your church’s preaching of the Word alongside this reading.

**Today’s reading — 2 Timothy 3:14–17 (NIV)**

> 14 But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it, 15 and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, 17 so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.

**Translation note**

- **Verse 15:** NIV “Holy Scriptures” / LSB “sacred writings.” Both translate *hiera grammata*. The wording differs, but both refer here to the sacred writings Timothy had known from childhood.
- **Verse 16:** NIV “useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting” / LSB “profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction.” These are largely vocabulary differences: “useful” and “profitable” express benefit, while “rebuking” and “reproof” describe exposing and confronting error.
- **Verse 17:** NIV “servant of God” / LSB “man of God.” The LSB preserves the traditional wording of the Greek expression. The NIV emphasizes the person’s role in serving God. Paul is addressing Timothy directly; the passage also shows how Scripture equips God’s people for good work.

**LSB (for comparison)**

> 14 But you, continue in the things you learned and became convinced of, knowing from whom you learned them, 15 and that from childhood you have known the sacred writings which are able to make you wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness, 17 so that the man of God may be equipped, having been thoroughly equipped for every good work.

**Reflection**

Where will you put even ten quiet minutes with Scripture this week so God’s Word can teach, correct, and train you—and so Jordyn, Elijah, and Enoch see their dad listening to the Father?

**Lesson 9: The Church, a Family That's Devoted Together**

Every lesson so far has been about your own walk: grace, prayer, Scripture. Today's reading shows that God never meant you to walk alone. Right after Pentecost, the first believers didn't just attend something. They *devoted themselves* to four things together: the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer. We receive the apostles' teaching through Scripture.

John Piper explains that the Greek word for fellowship, *koinonia*, comes from the word for “common”: “Koinonia (fellowship) means having things koina (in common).” That's why Luke goes straight on to say they shared what they had with anyone in need. Real fellowship goes deeper than coffee after service. It means caring enough that another person's need becomes your concern.

Notice the rhythm, too. They met in large gatherings at the temple and in homes around a table. For you, that can include Sunday at Grace Life and sharing life with church members during the week. Your dinner table with Sanqueta and the kids can reflect that same gladness, prayer, and generosity, though family life doesn't replace belonging to a church.

**Today's reading: Acts 2:42–47 (NIV)**

42 They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. 43 Everyone was filled with awe at the many wonders and signs performed by the apostles. 44 All the believers were together and had everything in common. 45 They sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need. 46 Every day they continued to meet together in the temple courts. They broke bread in their homes and ate together with glad and sincere hearts, 47 praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.

**Translation notes**

- **Verse 42:** NIV “to prayer” / LSB “to the prayers.” The Greek has the definite article and a plural. The LSB preserves that form, which ...on of baptized believers, associated by covenant.” It operates “under the Lordship of Christ through democratic processes,” with pastors and deacons as its officers. It also describes the church as the Body of Christ, “which includes all of the redeemed of all the ages.” In plain words, each local congregation governs its own affairs under Christ, while also belonging to the larger fellowship of God's people.

By comparison, the Catholic Catechism, paragraph 816, teaches that Christ's church “subsists in the Catholic Church, which is governed by the successor of Peter and by the bishops in communion with him.” That's a real difference in how church unity and authority are understood. It doesn't mean Catholic teaching denies that other Christians belong to Christ. We'll unpack these differences gradually, including Orthodox and other Protestant perspectives, without treating disagreement as a reason for disrespect.

**Go deeper**

- [The Fear of God and Freedom from Goods](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-fear-of-god-and-freedom-from-goods), John Piper's sermon on this passage, December 2, 1990.
- [Grace Life Doctrines](https://yourgracelife.com/doctrines), your church's statement on the Bible, God, salvation, and the church.
- [Acts: Church on the Move Part 2](https://yourgracelife.com/media/acts-church-on-the-move-part-2), an early sermon in Grace Life's Acts series; its exact passage wasn't confirmed.

**Reflection question**

What's one way this week you could make your family's table reflect the gladness and generosity of Acts 2—and is there someone in your church family whose need you could help carry?

**Lesson 10: Godly Manhood, Strong and Anchored in God's Word**

Good morning, Gregory. Today we start the "man, husband, father" part of the path. Notice what the Bible says makes a man strong: it isn't toughness or having it all together. God tells Joshua to be strong and courageous, and each time he gives the reason: "I will be with you." Courage comes from God's presence, not from our own nerve.

God also ties that strength to his Word. Joshua is told to keep it on his lips and think on it day and night, so he can obey it. A strong man, then, is one who stays near God, listens to him, and acts on what he hears. Paul adds the final piece: be strong, but "do everything in love." Strength without love hurts people, and love without strength can't protect them. A godly man carries both.

**Today's reading: Joshua 1:5–9 (NIV)**

5 No one will be able to stand against you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you. 6 Be strong and courageous, because you will lead these people to inherit the land I swore to their ancestors to give them. 7 "Be strong and very courageous. Be careful to obey all the law my servant Moses gave you; do not turn from it to the right or to the left, that you may be successful wherever you go. 8 Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it. Then you will be prosperous and successful. 9 Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the Lord your God will be with you wherever you go."

**1 Corinthians 16:13–14 (NIV)**

13 Be on your guard; stand firm in the faith; be courageous; be strong. 14 Do everything in love.

**Translation note**

*1 Corinthians 16:13.* The NIV says "be courageous," and the LSB says "act like men." The Greek word *andrizesthe* comes from the word for "man," so the LSB keeps that root visible, while the NIV gives the sense, which is courage. Both point to grown-up, brave faithfulness. Also, the NIV's "Be on your guard" and the LSB's "Be watchful" translate the same call to stay alert.

*Joshua 1:7–8.* The NIV says "Be careful to obey… do everything written in it," and the LSB says "be careful to do according to…" with a footnote that the Hebrew literally means "observe," as in guard or keep. Obeying is more than hearing; it means guarding God's Word and putting it into practice. The LSB footnote also notes that the Hebrew behind "successful" and "prosperous" can mean "act wisely," so in context, success is wise obedience, not just results.

*Joshua 1:9.* The NIV says "the Lord," and the LSB says "Yahweh." Both translate God's personal covenant name; the NIV uses the traditional title.

**Go deeper:** Tony Evans' book *Kingdom Man* fits this theme well. It's about a man living under God's authority and taking responsibility for his family and community.

**Reflection question:** Where do you most need "I will be with you" this week, at work, with Sanqueta, or with the kids? What's one concrete way to stay in God's Word so you act from his strength and not your own?

**Lesson 11: Marriage, loving your wife the way Christ loves the church**

Yesterday was about being a strong, courageous man anchored in God's Word. Today we look at where that strength gets tested most every day: at home, with your wife. Ephesians 5 is one of the best-known marriage passages in the Bible. It's also one of the most misunderstood.

Notice where Paul starts in verse 21: "Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ." Before he says anything to husbands or wives, he puts the whole household under Jesus. Then he gives each spouse a different calling. Wives are asked to submit to their husbands "as you do to the Lord." Husbands get the longer and heavier command: "love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her." The standard for a husband isn't how other men treat their wives. It's the cross.

John Piper preached two sermons on this passage. In the first he says headship "is not a right to control or to abuse or to neglect. (Christ's sacrifice is the pattern.) Rather, it's the responsibility to love like Christ in leading and protecting and providing for your wife and family." He defines headship as "the divine calling of a husband to take primary responsibility for Christ-like, servant leadership, protection, and provision in the home." He calls the Christian husband "lionhearted and lamblike," because Jesus is both the Lion of Judah and the Lamb of God (Revelation 5:5–6): "strong and meek, tough and tender."

Verses 28–29 make it concrete. A man feeds and cares for his own body without anyone having to remind him. Paul says to give your wife that same everyday, instinctive care, the way Christ keeps caring for his church. Verse 32 shows the bigger picture: your marriage is meant to be a small, living picture of Christ and his people that your kids and neighbors can watch.

**Today's reading: Ephesians 5:21–33 (NIV)**

21 Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.

22 Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands as you do to the Lord. 23 For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, his body, of which he is the Savior. 24 Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything.

25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her 26 to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, 27 and to present her to himself as a radiant church, without stain or wrinkle or any other blemish, but holy and blameless. 28 In this same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. 29 After all, no one ever hated their own body, but they feed and care for their body, just as Christ does the church— 30 for we are members of his body. 31 "For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh." 32 This is a profound mystery—but I am talking about Christ and the church. 33 However, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.

(NIV footnotes: v26 "cleansing" can also be read "having cleansed." v31 quotes Genesis 2:24.)

**Translation notes (LSB)**

- **Verse 21.** NIV: "Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ." LSB: "and being subject to one another in the fear of Christ." In Greek, verse 21 isn't a separate command. It's a participle ("being subject") that carries on Paul's sentence from verse 18, "be filled with the Spirit." The LSB keeps that grammar, so you can see mutual submission is one of the things a Spirit-filled life looks like. The NIV makes it its own sentence so it reads clearly in English. The noun is *phobos*, "fear." The LSB keeps "fear," and the NIV gives the sense as "reverence." The LSB's own footnote allows "reverence" too.
- **Verse 33.** NIV: "the wife must respect her husband." LSB: "the wife must see to it that she respects her husband." The LSB footnote says "respects" is literally "fear," and points back to verse 21. Paul uses the same word family for honoring Christ and for a wife honoring her husband. It means deep respect, not being afraid. The NIV gives the meaning, and the LSB footnote shows the link to verse 21.
- **Verse 29.** NIV: "no one ever hated their own body, but they feed and care for their body." LSB: "no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it." The Greek says "flesh," which the LSB keeps. That ties it to "one flesh" in verse 31. The NIV says "body" to match verse 28. "Cherishes" is a warm word that means keeping something warm and tenderly caring for it, and the LSB's wording brings out that tenderness a bit more.

**Going deeper**

- [Lionhearted and Lamblike: The Christian Husband as Head, Part 1](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/lionhearted-and-lamblike-the-christian-husband-as-head-part-1), John Piper, Mar 18, 2007
- [Lionhearted and Lamblike: What Does It Mean to Lead? Part 2](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/lionhearted-and-lamblike-the-christian-husband-as-head-part-2), John Piper, Mar 25, 2007
- Tony Evans' book *Kingdom Marriage* goes well with *Kingdom Man* from yesterday.

**Reflection question:** Verse 29 says to "feed and care for" your wife the way you naturally take care of yourself. What's one specific way you can nourish and cherish Sanqueta this week, without her asking, so that Jordyn, Elijah, and Enoch get a clear picture of how Christ loves his church?

**Lesson 12: Fatherhood: passing faith on at home**

Yesterday's lesson was about loving Sanqueta the way Christ loves the church. Today the focus moves to Jordyn, Elijah, and Enoch. God's plan for passing on faith isn't mainly a program or a class. It's a dad whose own heart is full of God's words, and those words come out in ordinary moments: at the dinner table, in the car, at bedtime, at breakfast. Deuteronomy 6 says it plainly. First, *"these commandments… are to be on your hearts."* Only after that comes *"impress them on your children."* You can't pass on what you don't carry yourself.

Ephesians 6:4 adds a warning and a calling. The warning is "do not exasperate your children." John Piper points out that of all the things Paul could have warned fathers about, he picked anger. Piper's reading is that fathers usually pass anger on by living with it themselves, and the cure is the gospel: being "kind… tenderhearted, forgiving… as God in Christ forgave you" (Ephesians 4:32). He's also clear that this verse doesn't make a dad passive. Kids are still called to obey. The point is to avoid things like nagging, harshness, and petty rules that don't connect to anything bigger. The calling is to "bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord." Piper says that means showing your kids something great to live for, so that when you say no, they can see it serves God's bigger purpose for them and not just your convenience.

Piper also notes that Paul says "Fathers" here, while the verse just before it says "parents." That gives dads the leading responsibility. He's careful to say it isn't the only responsibility.

**Today's reading (NIV)**

*Deuteronomy 6:4–9*
4 Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. 5 Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. 6 These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. 7 Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. 8 Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. 9 Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates.

*Ephesians 6:4*
4 Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

**Translation notes (LSB)**

- **Deuteronomy 6:7.** The NIV says "Impress them on your children," and the LSB says "You shall teach them diligently to your sons." The Hebrew verb carries the idea of sharpening, or repeating something until it sticks. The NIV goes with "impress" and the LSB with "teach diligently." The Hebrew word for "sons" is often used for children in general, so the NIV translates the sense ("children") and the LSB keeps the literal word ("sons").
- **Deuteronomy 6:8.** The NIV says "bind them on your foreheads," and the LSB says "they shall be as phylacteries between your eyes." The Hebrew word is rare. The NIV gives a general meaning ("symbols"), while the LSB uses "phylacteries," the small Scripture boxes Jewish men later wore to obey this verse. The LSB's footnote also gives "frontals."
- **Ephesians 6:4.** The NIV says "do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training," and the LSB says "do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline." The Greek verb has "anger" built into it, and the LSB spells that out. The Greek noun *paideia* covers both training and correction, so each translation brings out a different side of the same word. The NIV also has a footnote on "Fathers" that reads "Or *Parents*," because the Greek word can occasionally mean both parents.

**Go deeper**
- [Marriage Is Meant for Making Children… Disciples of Jesus, Part 2](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/marriage-is-meant-for-making-children-disciples-of-jesus-part-2), John Piper's sermon on Ephesians 6:4
- [More Thoughts for Fathers on Ephesians 6:4](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/more-thoughts-for-fathers-on-ephesians-6-4), a short Desiring God follow-up article

**Reflection**
When your kids look back on this week, would they say "Dad talked about God with me" in some ordinary moment, like the car ride, dinner, or bedtime? And is there one place, maybe a tone or a rule you keep repeating, where you might be stirring up anger in one of them instead of drawing them toward something bigger?

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 13: Baptism, buried with Christ and raised to walk in new life**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we talked about passing faith on at home. Today we look at the first public step of that faith: baptism. In Romans 6, Paul answers a fair question. If God's grace covers all our sin, why not keep sinning? His answer is that a believer has died to that old life. Baptism is the picture of that death and new beginning. You go down into the water like a burial and come up like a resurrection.

John Piper explains this in three steps in his sermon [United with Christ in Death and Life, Part 2](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/united-with-christ-in-death-and-life-part-2) (Oct 1, 2000). First, Christ died at Calvary, and God counted his death as ours. Second, we trusted Christ, and that death became personal to us. Third, we were baptized, which shows it publicly. In his words: "Accomplishment in history, application by faith, signification through baptism." He also calls baptism "an ordinance performed only once in the Christian's life" that "signifies our dying and rising with Christ by faith."

The practical point is verse 11. You don't have to strain to become dead to sin. In Christ you already are, so you "count" it true and live like it. When an old habit or temper pulls at you, you can tell yourself, "That man was buried. I don't live there anymore."

**Today's reading: Romans 6:1–11 (NIV)**

> 6 What shall we say, then? Shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase? 2 By no means! We are those who have died to sin; how can we live in it any longer? 3 Or don't you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? 4 We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.
>
> 5 For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we will certainly also be united with him in a resurrection like his. 6 For we know that our old self was crucified with him so that the body ruled by sin might be done away with, that we should no longer be slaves to sin— 7 because anyone who has died has been set free from sin.
>
> 8 Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him. 9 For we know that since Christ was raised from the dead, he cannot die again; death no longer has mastery over him. 10 The death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God.
>
> 11 In the same way, count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.

*NIV footnote on v6, "done away with": "Or be rendered powerless."*

**Translation notes (LSB)**

- **v4.** The NIV has "we too may live a new life." The LSB has "so we too might walk in newness of life." Paul's Greek verb means "to walk," a common Jewish way of describing how a person conducts their life. The LSB keeps the walking picture, and the NIV gives the meaning in plain modern English.
- **v6.** The NIV has "our old self… the body ruled by sin." The LSB has "our old man… our body of sin." The Greek says "old man" (*anthrōpos*), meaning the person you were before Christ, and "body of sin." The NIV reads that as "the body ruled by sin," and the LSB keeps the shorter phrase and leaves it to the reader. Both translations note that "done away with" can also mean "made powerless."
- **v7.** The NIV has "has been set free from sin." The LSB has "has been justified from sin," with a footnote: "Or acquitted." The Greek verb (*dikaioō*) is the one usually translated "justify." Here it carries the sense of being released from sin's claim, like a dead man the law can no longer charge. The NIV puts that result into words, and the LSB keeps the legal word.

**A brief look at how Christians understand baptism**

Christians broadly agree that Jesus commanded baptism ("Go… make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them," Matthew 28:19) and that it is tied to union with Christ. They differ on what baptism does and who should receive it.

- **Grace Life (Baptist).** Grace Life's [Doctrines page](https://yourgracelife.com/doctrines) describes the church as a congregation "of baptized believers" observing "the two ordinances of Christ." "Ordinance" means a practice Christ commanded us to obey. Piper, himself a Baptist, holds the same believer's-baptism view. He argues that baptism follows faith, that it pictures what faith has already received, and that immersion best shows Romans 6:4's burial and resurrection.
- **Catholic Church (in its own words).** The Catechism, paragraph 1213, calls baptism a sacrament: "Through Baptism we are freed from sin and reborn as sons of God." In that view, baptism is God's means of giving new life, not only a sign of it.

These are real differences, and there are differences within traditions too. They're worth understanding with respect, not arguing over.

**Reflection question:** Your kids watch how you live more than what you say. What is one "old man" habit, like a short temper, a screen habit, or a sharp word, that you can treat as buried this week so they see what "walking in newness of life" looks like?

# Grace, the foundation of everything

**Date:** Saturday, October 31, 2026
**Scripture:** Ephesians 2:1–10
**Translation used:** NIV

Before you take up any other lesson in this track — who God is, who you are as a woman, how to pray, how to love a husband or a child — start here. Grace is the foundation. You do not build a life with God by proving yourself useful, pretty, organized, or strong enough. You receive a gift.

## The passage (NIV)

1 As for you, you were dead in your transgressions and sins, 2 in which you used to live when you followed the ways of this world and of the ruler of the kingdom of the air, the spirit who is now at work in those who are disobedient. 3 All of us also lived among them at one time, gratifying the cravings of our flesh and following its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature deserving of wrath. 4 But because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, 5 made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in transgressions—it is by grace you have been saved. 6 And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus, 7 in order that in the coming ages he might show the incomparable riches of his grace, expressed in his kindness to us in Christ Jesus. 8 For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God— 9 not by works, so that no one can boast. 10 For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.

## What this is saying

Paul does not start with your gifts or your roles. He starts with a hard truth: without Christ, we were dead, not merely discouraged. That is true of women and of men. Then comes the mercy: “But because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ.” Grace is God doing for you what you could not do for yourself.

Verses 8–9 take the weight off your performance. Salvation is a gift. You cannot earn a father’s welcome by keeping a beautiful home, by never missing a quiet time, or by being the woman everyone needs. Good works matter — verse 10 says you are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works he prepared. But those works are the fruit of grace, not the root of it.

Priscilla Shirer, who teaches with Going Beyond Ministries and is Tony Evans’s daughter, often comes back to this same center: the Christian life is a response to what God has already done, not a way of getting him to notice you. Her teaching on prayer and on the Spirit starts with people who already belong to Jesus. We are not quoting a single line from her here, because we could not pin one short sentence to a public page with enough certainty, but that is the pattern of her ministry, and it matches Ephesians 2.

## Go deeper

- [Ephesians 2:1–10 on Bible Gateway (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ephesians+2%3A1-10&version=NIV)
- [Going Beyond Ministries](https://goingbeyond.com/ministry/)

## How this applies

If you are tired of trying to be enough, this passage is for you. Receive the gift. Then walk, as a living woman, into the good works God already prepared — not to be loved, but because you are.

## Reflection

Where have you been trying to earn what God has already given you in Christ? What would it look like, today, to receive grace as a gift and then do the next good work from rest, not from fear?

LSB notes: The Legacy Standard Bible often uses “Yahweh” where the NIV has “the Lord,” and “Messiah” or a more literal wording in some New Testament lines. The meaning of the verses in these lessons is the same.

---

# Who God Is

**Date:** Sunday, November 1, 2026
**Scripture:** Exodus 34:6–7; Isaiah 6:1–5; 1 John 4:8–10
**Translation used:** NIV

If grace is the foundation, you need to know the God who gives it. He is not an idea you shape to fit your feelings. He has told you his name.

## The passages (NIV)

**Exodus 34:6–7**
6 And he passed in front of Moses, proclaiming, “The Lord, the Lord, the compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness, 7 maintaining love to thousands, and forgiving wickedness, rebellion and sin. Yet he does not leave the guilty unpunished; he punishes the children and their children for the sin of the parents to the third and fourth generation.”

**Isaiah 6:1–5**
1 In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord, high and exalted, seated on a throne; and the train of his robe filled the temple. 2 Above him were seraphim, each with six wings: With two wings they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they were flying. 3 And they were calling to one another: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Almighty; the whole earth is full of his glory.” 4 At the sound of their voices the doorposts and thresholds shook and the temple was filled with smoke. 5 “Woe to me!” I cried. “I am ruined! For I am a man of unclean lips, and I live among a people of unclean lips, and my eyes have seen the King, the Lord Almighty.”

**1 John 4:8–10**
8 Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love. 9 This is how God showed his love among us: He sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him. 10 This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.

## What this is saying

God names himself: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness — and also just. He does not leave the guilty unpunished. His holiness is not a harsh mood; it is his blazing purity. Isaiah does not stroll into that throne room feeling affirmed. He says, “Woe to me.”

And this same God is love. John will not let you shrink love into a warm feeling. “This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.” The God who is holy is the God who comes near in Christ.

Anne Graham Lotz, Billy Graham’s daughter, has spent her life calling women and men to this God as he has spoken in Scripture. She writes, “God’s Word doesn’t change. And you can build your life on it knowing that God’s Word works.” ([The Power of Our Example](https://annegrahamlotz.org/2021/05/06/the-power-of-our-example/)) You do not have to invent a god you can manage. You can build your life on the God who has spoken.

## Go deeper

- [Exodus 34:6–7 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+34%3A6-7&version=NIV)
- [Anne Graham Lotz, “The Power of Our Example”](https://annegrahamlotz.org/2021/05/06/the-power-of-our-example/)

## How this applies

When fear or shame names God for you, go back to his own words. He is holy and he is love. Both are true at once, and both are good for you.

## Reflection

Which side of God’s name do you quietly drop — his holiness, or his love? What would it look like to trust both today?

# Who Jesus Is

**Date:** Monday, November 2, 2026
**Scripture:** John 1:1–14; Colossians 1:15–20; Hebrews 1:1–3
**Translation used:** NIV

The God who is holy and loving has a face. His name is Jesus. Everything in this study hangs on who he is, not only on what he can do for your week.

## The passages (NIV)

**John 1:1–4, 14**
1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. 2 He was with God in the beginning. 3 Through him all things were made; without him nothing was made that has been made. 4 In him was life, and that life was the light of all mankind.

14 The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us. We have seen his glory, the glory of the one and only Son, who came from the Father, full of grace and truth.

**Colossians 1:15–20**
15 The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. 16 For in him all things were created: things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or powers or rulers or authorities; all things have been created through him and for him. 17 He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. 18 And he is the head of the body, the church; he is the beginning and the firstborn from among the dead, so that in everything he might have the supremacy. 19 For God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him, 20 and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through his blood, shed on the cross.

**Hebrews 1:1–3**
1 In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets at many times and in various ways, 2 but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, and through whom also he made the universe. 3 The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of his being, sustaining all things by his powerful word. After he had provided purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty in heaven.

## What this is saying

Jesus is not only a teacher, a friend, or a helper for hard days — though he is a friend. He is the Word who was with God and was God. He became flesh. He holds all things together. He made peace by his blood. After he provided purification for sins, he sat down. The work is finished.

That means a woman’s hope is not first in a husband, a child, a ministry, or her own grit. Your hope is a Person who is God with us, and who has already dealt with sin.

Elisabeth Elliot, whose life and teaching John Piper has long recommended, prayed to be a woman who received from God whatever he chose to give. Piper quotes her: “We are women, and my plea is Let me be a woman, holy through and through, asking for nothing but what God wants to give me, receiving with both hands and with all my heart whatever that is.” ([Peaches in Paradise](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/peaches-in-paradise)) The first gift God gives is his Son. Receive him with both hands.

## Go deeper

- [John 1:1–14 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+1%3A1-14&version=NIV)
- [John Piper on Elisabeth Elliot](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/peaches-in-paradise)

## How this applies

When you are tempted to treat Jesus as one resource among many, come back to these texts. He is the center. Every other gift in your life is held together by him.

## Reflection

In what part of your life have you been asking Jesus only to help, rather than to be Lord? What would it look like to receive him with both hands today?

# Sin and Forgiveness, Walking in the Light

**Date:** Tuesday, November 3, 2026
**Scripture:** 1 John 1:5–9; Psalm 51:1–12; Romans 3:23–24
**Translation used:** NIV

Grace does not pretend you are fine. It brings you into the light, where sin is named and forgiven.

## The passages (NIV)

**1 John 1:5–9**
5 This is the message we have heard from him and declare to you: God is light; in him there is no darkness at all. 6 If we claim to have fellowship with him and yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not live out the truth. 7 But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, purifies us from all sin. 8 If we claim to be without sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. 9 If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness.

**Psalm 51:1–2, 10**
1 Have mercy on me, O God, according to your unfailing love; according to your great compassion blot out my transgressions. 2 Wash away all my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin.

10 Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.

**Romans 3:23–24**
23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, 24 and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.

## What this is saying

There is no special women’s sin and men’s sin at the root. “All have sinned.” A woman’s temptations may often run toward comparison, control, people-pleasing, bitterness, or hidden impurity, just as a man’s may run toward pride, lust, or passivity — but the problem is the same: we fall short of God’s glory. Hiding it is the darkness. Confessing it is the way into fellowship.

Forgiveness is not God waving a feeling over you. It is God being “faithful and just.” The blood of Jesus really purifies. You can tell the truth without being crushed, because the cross has already told the truth about your sin and paid for it.

## Go deeper

- [1 John 1:5–9 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+John+1%3A5-9&version=NIV)
- [Psalm 51 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm+51&version=NIV)

## How this applies

Is there something you have been managing in the dark — a resentment, a habit, a hidden screen, a story you tell yourself about someone? Bring it into the light with God, and, where it is wise, with a trusted sister or with your husband.

## Reflection

What would walking in the light look like for you this week — not later, and not in general, but with one honest confession?

# Faith and Repentance, Coming Home to the Father

**Date:** Wednesday, November 4, 2026
**Scripture:** Luke 15:11–24; Mark 1:14–15; Acts 3:19
**Translation used:** NIV

Faith is not a vague optimism. It is coming home. Repentance is the turn that faith takes when it believes the Father is good.

## The passages (NIV)

**Mark 1:14–15**
14 After John was put in prison, Jesus went into Galilee, proclaiming the good news of God. 15 “The time has come,” he said. “The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news!”

**Acts 3:19**
19 Repent, then, and turn to God, so that your sins may be wiped out, that times of refreshing may come from the Lord.

**Luke 15:20–24**
20 So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him. 21 The son said to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” 22 But the father said to his servants, “Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. 23 Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let’s have a feast and celebrate. 24 For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.” So they began to celebrate.

## What this is saying

Jesus joins two words that some of us pull apart: repent and believe. Repentance is not self-hatred. It is turning around. Faith is not a feeling you try to inflate. It is trusting the good news enough to come home.

The father in Jesus’ story runs. He does not make the child earn the porch. If you have wandered — in obvious ways or in quiet, respectable ones — the way back is the same. Get up and go to your Father. He is not waiting to shame you. He is waiting to embrace you.

## Go deeper

- [Luke 15:11–32 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+15%3A11-32&version=NIV)

## How this applies

Coming home may mean a first turning to Christ, or it may mean a fresh turning in a place you have been managing on your own. Either way, the Father’s welcome is the same.

## Reflection

Where do you need to get up and go to the Father today? What keeps you standing a long way off?

# The Holy Spirit, the Helper Who Stays With You

**Date:** Thursday, November 5, 2026
**Scripture:** John 14:16–26; Galatians 5:22–25; Romans 8:14–16
**Translation used:** NIV

You are not asked to live the Christian life as a solo project. Jesus promised another Helper, the Spirit of truth, who stays with you.

## The passages (NIV)

**John 14:16–17, 26**
16 And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another advocate to help you and be with you forever— 17 the Spirit of truth. The world cannot accept him, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you know him, for he lives with you and will be in you.

26 But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have said to you.

**Galatians 5:22–25**
22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. 24 Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. 25 Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit.

**Romans 8:14–16**
14 For those who are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God. 15 The Spirit you received does not make you slaves, so that you live in fear again; rather, the Spirit you received brought about your adoption to sonship. And by him we cry, “Abba, Father.” 16 The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children.

## What this is saying

The Spirit is not a mood or a force. He is a Person — the Helper who teaches, reminds, leads, and bears fruit in you. Adoption is his gift. He teaches your heart to say “Abba, Father,” which is as true for a daughter as it is for a son.

The fruit in Galatians 5 is not a personality type. A quiet woman and a strong, entrepreneurial woman can both keep in step with the Spirit. Love, patience, faithfulness, and self-control are his work in you, including in hidden work at home.

Priscilla Shirer has spent much of her public teaching helping women take the Holy Spirit seriously as a Person who lives in them and who is enough for ordinary obedience. Her Going Beyond ministry, tied to the Evans family, keeps coming back to that: you are not left on your own to produce a holy life.

You do not have to manufacture fruit. Ask the Spirit to lead you in the next conversation, the next task, the next temptation. Keep in step, one ordinary hour at a time.

Where have you been trying to produce fruit in your own strength? What would it look like to ask the Helper to lead you there today?

# Prayer, Talking With Your Father

**Date:** Friday, November 6, 2026
**Scripture:** Matthew 6:5–13; Philippians 4:6–7; James 5:16
**Translation used:** NIV

Prayer is not a performance and it is not a last resort. It is a daughter talking with her Father.

## The passages (NIV)

**Matthew 6:6–13**
6 But when you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen. Then your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. 7 And when you pray, do not keep on babbling like pagans, for they think they will be heard because of their many words. 8 Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

9 “This, then, is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, 10 your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. 11 Give us today our daily bread. 12 And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. 13 And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’”

**Philippians 4:6–7**
6 Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. 7 And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

**James 5:16**
16 Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective.

## What this is saying

Jesus teaches a hidden life of prayer. Your Father already knows what you need. You still ask, because prayer is relationship, not information. You hallow his name, seek his kingdom, ask for daily bread, confess, forgive, and ask for deliverance.

Anxiety is not solved by more circling thoughts. It is brought to God “in every situation,” with thanksgiving. His peace then guards you.

Priscilla Shirer’s book *Fervent* (Moody Publishers) calls women to targeted, urgent, Scripture-shaped prayer — not as a way to impress God, but as a way to fight for their families and their own hearts. We paraphrase her emphasis here rather than force a sentence we could not verify word-for-word on a public page: prayer is a real work, and it is effective because God is faithful, not because you found the perfect wording. Anne Graham Lotz, in the same way, keeps pointing people back to God’s unchanging Word as the place you stand when you pray ([The Power of Our Example](https://annegrahamlotz.org/2021/05/06/the-power-of-our-example/)).

## Go deeper

- [Fervent, Moody Publishers](https://www.moodypublishers.com/fervent/)

## How this applies

You do not need a long, public prayer life to begin. Close the door. Use Jesus’ words if your own feel thin. Pray for your people by name.

## Reflection

What anxiety or person will you actually bring to the Father today, in secret, with thanksgiving?

# Reading Scripture — God-breathed words that equip you

**Date:** Saturday, November 7, 2026
**Scripture:** 2 Timothy 3:14–17; Psalm 19:7–11; Psalm 119:105
**Translation used:** NIV

God has not left you to guess. He has spoken, and his words are enough to make you wise for salvation and equipped for every good work — including the hidden ones.

## The passages (NIV)

**2 Timothy 3:14–17**
14 But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it, 15 and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, 17 so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.

**Psalm 19:7–11**
7 The law of the Lord is perfect, refreshing the soul. The statutes of the Lord are trustworthy, making wise the simple. 8 The precepts of the Lord are right, giving joy to the heart. The commands of the Lord are radiant, giving light to the eyes. 9 The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever. The decrees of the Lord are firm, and all of them are righteous. 10 They are more precious than gold, than much pure gold; they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the honeycomb. 11 By them your servant is warned; in keeping them there is great reward.

**Psalm 119:105**
105 Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.

## What this is saying

Timothy learned the Scriptures from infancy, and Paul names the people who taught him — which, in his case, included his mother and grandmother (2 Timothy 1:5). A woman’s voice, teaching the Bible in the home, is not small. The same God-breathed Word that saves also trains.

You do not have to be a scholar to begin. Read a short passage slowly. Ask what it says about God, about you, and about the next step of obedience. Let it rebuke and correct you, not only comfort you.

Anne Graham Lotz writes, “God’s Word doesn’t change. And you can build your life on it knowing that God’s Word works.” She also recalls the inscription her mother, Ruth Bell Graham, wrote in a Bible: “Read it, study it, love it, live it.” ([The Power of Our Example](https://annegrahamlotz.org/2021/05/06/the-power-of-our-example/)) That is a whole life’s plan in one line.

## Go deeper

- [2 Timothy 3:14–17 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2+Timothy+3%3A14-17&version=NIV)
- [Anne Graham Lotz, “The Power of Our Example”](https://annegrahamlotz.org/2021/05/06/the-power-of-our-example/)

## How this applies

Set a small, steady time with an open Bible — even if it is short, and even if a child interrupts it. The aim is not a perfect routine. The aim is to keep coming to God-breathed words.

## Reflection

What would “read it, study it, love it, live it” look like in your actual week, not in an ideal one?

You were not saved to walk alone. God places daughters in a family called the church.

## The passages (NIV)

**Acts 2:42–47**
42 They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. 43 Everyone was filled with awe at the many wonders and signs performed by the apostles. 44 All the believers were together and had everything in common. 45 They sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need. 46 Every day they continued to meet together in the temple courts. 9 Love must be sincere. Hate what is evil; cling to what is good. 10 Be devoted to one another in love. ## What this is saying

The first church was devoted: to the Word, to one another, to the table, and to prayer. That devotion is not less than a Sunday gathering, and it is more than a Sunday gathering. Homes matter. # Godly Womanhood, Strength and a Quiet Trust

**Date:** Monday, November 9, 2026
**Scripture:** Proverbs 31:10–31; Titus 2:3–5; 1 Peter 3:1–6
**Translation used:** NIV

Godly womanhood is not fragility, and it is not a copy of manhood. It is strength under God, a holy trust, and a life that does good.

## The passages (NIV)

**Proverbs 31:10–12, 25–31**
10 A wife of noble character who can find? She is worth far more than rubies. 11 Her husband has full confidence in her and lacks nothing of value. 12 She brings him good, not harm, all the days of her life.

25 She is clothed with strength and dignity; she can laugh at the days to come. 26 She speaks with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue. 27 She watches over the affairs of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness. 28 Her children arise and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her: 29 “Many women do noble things, but you surpass them all.” 30 Charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting; but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised. 31 Honor her for all that her hands have done, and let her works bring her praise at the city gate.

**Titus 2:3–5**
3 Likewise, teach the older women to be reverent in the way they live, not to be slanderers or addicted to much wine, but to teach what is good. 4 Then they can urge the younger women to love their husbands and children, 5 to be self-controlled and pure, to be busy at home, to be kind, and to be subject to their husbands, so that no one will malign the word of God.

**1 Peter 3:1–6**
1 Wives, in the same way submit yourselves to your own husbands so that, if any of them do not believe the word, they may be won over without words by the behavior of their wives, 2 when they see the purity and reverence of your lives. 3 Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as elaborate hairstyles and the wearing of gold jewelry or fine clothes. 4 Rather, it should be that of your inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great worth in God’s sight. 5 For this is the way the holy women of the past who put their hope in God used to adorn themselves. They submitted themselves to their own husbands, 6 like Sarah, who obeyed Abraham and called him her lord. You are her daughters if you do what is right and do not give way to fear.

## What this is saying

Proverbs 31 is not a checklist for crushing yourself. It is a portrait of a woman who fears the Lord: strong, wise, industrious, generous, and a blessing to her household. Charm and beauty are not the measure. The fear of the Lord is.

Titus 2 gives the church a beautiful pattern: older women, living reverent lives, teaching what is good to younger women — love, self-control, purity, kindness, and a well-ordered home. This is not a slight. It is discipleship, woman to woman.

1 Peter 3 speaks of a gentle and quiet spirit. That is not silence or smallness. It is a settled hope in God that does not give way to fear. Sarah is named as a daughter-line for women who do what is right.

This is the complementarian vision taught at Grace Life and in the stream of pastors such as John Piper and Tony Evans: men and women are equal in dignity, and they are not interchangeable in every calling. A woman’s holy strength often looks like helping, nurturing, teaching what is good, and, in marriage, a glad, intelligent submission to her own husband’s servant leadership. That teaching is offered here with respect, not as a weapon.

Elisabeth Elliot, recommended by Piper, said: “We are women, and my plea is Let me be a woman, holy through and through, asking for nothing but what God wants to give me, receiving with both hands and with all my heart whatever that is.” ([Peaches in Paradise](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/peaches-in-paradise)) Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth, summarizing the True Woman Manifesto, has taught: “When we respond humbly to the male leadership in our homes and our churches, we demonstrate a noble submission to authority that reflects Christ’s submission to God His Father.” ([Revive Our Hearts](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/what-submission-does-and-does-not-mean-1/)) Submission in Scripture is never a call to follow a husband into sin, and it is never an excuse for a man to be harsh.

## Go deeper

- [Proverbs 31:10–31 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Proverbs+31%3A10-31&version=NIV)
- [Elisabeth Elliot, quoted by John Piper](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/peaches-in-paradise)
- [Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth on submission](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/what-submission-does-and-does-not-mean-1/)

## How this applies

Ask God to make you a woman, holy through and through — strong and gentle, useful and unhurried in your fear of the Lord. If you are younger, seek an older woman who can teach what is good. If you are older, do not bury that calling.

## Reflection

Where is God asking you to receive being a woman as a gift — with both hands — rather than resenting it, hiding it, or turning it into a performance?
