# Marriage, respecting and helping your husband as the church does Christ

**Date:** Tuesday, November 10, 2026
**Scripture:** Ephesians 5:21–33
**Translation used:** NIV

Christian marriage is not a contest for control. It is a living picture of Christ and the church. This lesson looks at that picture from the wife’s side.

## The passage (NIV)

**Ephesians 5:21–33**
21 Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.

22 Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands as you do to the Lord. 23 For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, his body, of which he is the Savior. 24 Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything.

25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her 26 to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, 27 and to present her to himself as a radiant church, without stain or wrinkle or any other blemish, but holy and blameless. 28 In this same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. 29 After all, no one ever hated their own body, but they feed and care for their body, just as Christ does the church— 30 for we are members of his body. 31 “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” 32 This is a profound mystery—but I am talking about Christ and the church. 33 However, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.

## What this is saying

Verse 21 sets the tone: both husband and wife submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. Then Paul gives each a particular call. The husband’s is costly love. The wife’s is respectful submission to her own husband, “as the church submits to Christ.”

This is not the erasure of a wife’s mind, gifts, or voice. A Proverbs 31 wife has her husband’s full confidence. She does him good, not harm, all the days of her life. Helping him is strong, intelligent work. Respect is not flattery. It is honoring the office God has given him and making it easier, not harder, for him to lead in love.

Ruth Bell Graham, who shared a long marriage with Billy Graham, is remembered for this line: “A happy marriage is the union of two good forgivers.” ([Billy Graham Library](https://billygrahamlibrary.org/what-makes-a-marriage-work/)) Forgiveness will matter as much as any skill. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth has taught that a wife’s humble response to godly leadership “reflects Christ’s submission to God His Father.” ([Revive Our Hearts](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/what-submission-does-and-does-not-mean-1/))

A hard but needed word: this passage is never a covering for abuse, and it never asks a wife to sin. If you are in danger, get safe help. A husband’s headship is patterned on Christ the Savior, who gave himself up — not on a man who uses his wife.

## Go deeper

- [Ephesians 5:21–33 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ephesians+5%3A21-33&version=NIV)
- [“What Makes a Marriage Work?”](https://billygrahamlibrary.org/what-makes-a-marriage-work/)

## How this applies

Ask, “What would do my husband good today? What would respect look like in our actual conversations?” If you need to forgive, or to ask forgiveness, do not wait for a perfect mood.

## Reflection

Where can you offer your husband respect and help this week in a way that is honest, specific, and free of bitterness?

# Motherhood: passing faith on at home

**Date:** Wednesday, November 11, 2026
**Scripture:** 2 Timothy 1:5; Deuteronomy 6:4–9; Psalm 127:3–5; Proverbs 31:26–28
**Translation used:** NIV

If God has given you children, the home is one of the first places faith is either passed on or quietly neglected. Motherhood is not a side story in the kingdom of God.

## The passages (NIV)

**2 Timothy 1:5**
5 I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, now lives in you also.

**Deuteronomy 6:4–9**
4 Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. 5 Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. 6 These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. 7 Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. 8 Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. 9 Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates.

**Psalm 127:3–5**
3 Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him. 4 Like arrows in the hands of a warrior are children born in one’s youth. 5 Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. They will not be put to shame when they contend with their opponents in court.

**Proverbs 31:26–28**
26 She speaks with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue. 27 She watches over the affairs of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness. 28 Her children arise and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her.

## What this is saying

Timothy’s sincere faith first lived in a grandmother and a mother. God often uses a woman’s ordinary, repeated words to plant a life of faith. Deuteronomy 6 is not a once-a-week lesson only. It is talk at the table, on the road, at bedtime, in the morning. The commands must be on your heart first, or they will not be impressed on your children.

Children are a heritage, not an interruption. That does not mean the days are easy. It means the work has weight.

Gloria Furman, writing for Desiring God, said: “Because motherhood is missional, there’s something of eternal value taking place in the realm of the unseen.” ([Missional Motherhood](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/missional-motherhood)) The unseen hours count.

Lois Evans, Tony Evans’s late wife and ministry partner, spent decades investing in family and in women; we are not attaching a quote to her name here, because we could not verify one on a public page with enough certainty. Her life still stands as a testimony that a woman’s partnership in the gospel and in the home can bear fruit for generations. You can read a remembrance of her work at [tonyevans.org/lois-evans](https://tonyevans.org/lois-evans/).

## Go deeper

- [2 Timothy 1:3–7 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2+Timothy+1%3A3-7&version=NIV)
- [Gloria Furman, “Missional Motherhood”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/missional-motherhood)
- [Lois Evans](https://tonyevans.org/lois-evans/)

## How this applies

You do not have to turn every hour into a formal lesson. Put the Word on your own heart, then talk about it as you go. One sincere conversation, one prayer at bedtime, one apology to a child, is real ministry.

## Reflection

What unseen, missional moment is in front of you today with your child — and how will you meet it with the Word on your heart?

# Baptism, buried with Christ and raised to walk in new life

**Date:** Thursday, November 12, 2026
**Scripture:** Matthew 28:18–20; Romans 6:3–4; Acts 2:38–41
**Translation used:** NIV

Baptism is not a style of church or a family tradition only. It is the public sign that you have died with Christ and been raised to walk in new life.

## The passages (NIV)

**Matthew 28:18–20**
18 Then Jesus came to them and said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. 19 Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, 20 and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.”

**Romans 6:3–4**
3 Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? 4 We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.

**Acts 2:38–41**
38 Peter replied, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. 39 The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off—for all whom the Lord our God will call.” 40 With many other words he warned them; and he pleaded with them, “Save yourselves from this corrupt generation.” 41 Those who accepted his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to their number that day.

## What this is saying

Jesus commands baptism as part of making disciples. It is in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Romans 6 explains the meaning: burial with Christ, and a raised life. The old life is not just improved. It is left in the tomb, and you walk out in newness.

Churches differ on the timing and mode of baptism — some baptize believing adults and older children, some also baptize the infants of believers as a sign of the covenant. This lesson does not pretend those differences are small, and it does not treat sisters in either practice as outsiders. What must not be lost is the gospel the sign points to: repentance, faith, forgiveness, and a new walk.

If you have trusted Christ and have not been baptized, this is a clear next step of obedience. If you have been baptized, remember what it meant. You do not live as if the old life still owns you.

## Go deeper

- [Romans 6:1–14 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans+6%3A1-14&version=NIV)
- [Matthew 28:16–20 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+28%3A16-20&version=NIV)

## How this applies

Remember your baptism, or take the step if you have delayed it. Walk today as a woman who has already been raised with Christ.

## Reflection

What would “walking in new life” look like in one concrete place where you are still living as if the old life were in charge?

# How the Bible is organized

**Scripture:** Luke 24:27; 2 Timothy 3:16
**Translation used:** NIV

The Bible is one book, and it is a library. It has 66 books, written by many human authors over many centuries, and one divine Author who breathes out all of it.

## The passages (NIV)

**Luke 24:27**
27 And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he explained to them what was said in all the Scriptures concerning himself.

**2 Timothy 3:16**
16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness.

## The big map

The **Old Testament** (39 books) tells of creation, the fall, God’s promises to Israel, and the long wait for the Messiah. It is often grouped this way:

- **Law** (5): Genesis–Deuteronomy
- **History** (12): Joshua–Esther
- **Poetry and Wisdom** (5): Job–Song of Songs
- **Major Prophets** (5): Isaiah–Daniel
- **Minor Prophets** (12): Hosea–Malachi (“minor” means shorter, not less important)

The **New Testament** (27 books) tells of Jesus, the beginning of the church, and the hope of his return:

- **Gospels** (4): Matthew, Mark, Luke, John
- **History** (1): Acts
- **Paul’s Letters** (13): Romans–Philemon
- **General Letters** (8): Hebrews–Jude
- **Prophecy** (1): Revelation

This app includes a card for each of the 66 books — author, date, theme, a key verse, and how the book points to Christ. Use this lesson as the map, then browse the reference whenever you need it.

Jesus read the Old Testament as a book about himself. That is how you should read it too: not as a random stack of sayings, but as one story that leads to Christ.

## Go deeper

- Open the **Books of the Bible** reference in this Grown-ups section.
- [Luke 24:13–35 (NIV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+24%3A13-35&version=NIV)

## Reflection

When you open your Bible this week, can you name which section you are in, and how that book might point to Jesus?

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
# The big storyline: creation to new creation

**Scripture:** Genesis 1:1; Genesis 3:15; Galatians 4:4–5; Revelation 21:1–5
**Translation used:** NIV

If you only read the Bible in fragments, you can miss the story. Here is the spine that holds the 66 books together.

## The passages (NIV)

**Genesis 1:1**
1 In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.

**Genesis 3:15**
15 “And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”

**Galatians 4:4–5**
4 But when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, 5 to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption to sonship.

**Revelation 21:1, 3–5**
1 Then I saw “a new heaven and a new earth,” for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and there was no longer any sea.

3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Look! God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. 4 ‘He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death’ or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.” 5 He who was seated on the throne said, “I am making everything new!”

## The six movements

1. **Creation.** God makes a good world and makes people in his image, to know him and care for his world.
2. **Fall.** Human sin breaks fellowship with God. Death and sorrow enter. God already promises an offspring who will crush the serpent.
3. **Israel.** God chooses Abraham, forms a people, gives the law, the land, the kings, and the prophets. They keep failing, and God keeps promising a faithful King and a new covenant.
4. **Christ.** In the fullness of time, God sends his Son. Jesus lives the faithful life Israel (and we) did not live, dies for sin, and rises.
5. **Church.** The risen Christ pours out the Spirit and gathers a people from all nations to witness until he comes.
6. **New creation.** Jesus will return. God will wipe away every tear and dwell with his people forever.

Every book you read sits somewhere on this line. Ask, “Where am I in the story, and what does this show me about the God who finishes what he started?”

## Reflection

Where do you usually live in this story — stuck at the fall, busy in the church age, or forgetful of the ending? How does the whole line steady you today?

# The covenants: God’s binding promises

**Scripture:** Genesis 12:1–3; Exodus 19:4–6; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Luke 22:20
**Translation used:** NIV

A covenant is a solemn, binding promise. The Bible’s story is held together by the covenants God makes — and keeps.

## The passages (NIV)

**Genesis 12:2–3**
2 “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing. 3 I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you.”

**Exodus 19:5–6**
5 “Now if you obey me fully and keep my covenant, then out of all nations you will be my treasured possession. Although the whole earth is mine, 6 you will be for me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.”

**2 Samuel 7:16**
16 “Your house and your kingdom will endure forever before me; your throne will be established forever.”

**Jeremiah 31:33–34**
33 “This is the covenant I will make with the people of Israel after that time,” declares the Lord. “I will put my law in their minds and write it on their hearts. I will be their God, and they will be my people. 34 … For I will forgive their wickedness and will remember their sins no more.”

**Luke 22:20**
20 In the same way, after the supper he took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.”

## A simple map of the covenants

Christians describe the covenants with slightly different outlines, but these are the main ones most evangelical teachers trace:

- **Noah** (Genesis 9): God preserves the world; the rainbow is the sign.
- **Abraham** (Genesis 12, 15, 17): land, offspring, and blessing for the nations; circumcision is the sign.
- **Sinai / Moses** (Exodus 19–24): God makes Israel his treasured people and gives the law.
- **David** (2 Samuel 7): an everlasting throne in David’s line.
- **The new covenant** (Jeremiah 31; Luke 22): forgiven hearts, the Spirit, and God’s law written within — sealed in Jesus’ blood.

There is also the first promise in the garden, sometimes called the covenant of grace already breaking in: the offspring will crush the serpent (Genesis 3:15). All of these roads run toward Christ. He is Abraham’s offspring, the true Israelite, the Son of David, and the mediator of the new covenant.

## Reflection

Which of these promises do you most need to remember — that God preserves, that he blesses the nations, that he has a King, or that he forgives and writes his law on the heart?

# Reading the Bible by genre

**Scripture:** Psalm 1:1–3; 2 Peter 1:19–21
**Translation used:** NIV

All Scripture is God-breathed, but it is not all the same kind of writing. You read a proverb differently than you read a gospel, and a psalm differently than a law.

## The passages (NIV)

**Psalm 1:1–3**
1 Blessed is the one who does not walk in step with the wicked or stand in the way that sinners take or sit in the company of mockers, 2 but whose delight is in the law of the Lord, and who meditates on his law day and night. 3 That person is like a tree planted by streams of water, which yields its fruit in season and whose leaf does not wither—whatever they do prospers.

**2 Peter 1:20–21**
20 Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture came about by the prophet’s own interpretation of things. 21 For prophecy never had its origin in the human will, but prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

## A short reading guide

- **Narrative** (Genesis, the Gospels, Acts): Ask what happened, what it shows about God, and how it fits the big story. Do not treat every action as a command for you.
- **Law**: See God’s holiness, Israel’s life as his people, and the need for a Savior. Christ fulfills the law; he does not toss it aside.
- **Poetry and Psalms**: Pray them. Let metaphors work as metaphors. The psalms give you words for joy, grief, repentance, and hope.
- **Wisdom** (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Job): Proverbs are generally true, not mechanical promises. Job and Ecclesiastes wrestle when life is hard or empty.
- **Prophecy**: Hear the original word to that people, the warnings and promises, and then how it is fulfilled in Christ — already, and not yet.
- **Letters**: Read whole arguments, not only favorite verses. Note who is writing, and what the church needed.
- **Apocalypse** (Revelation, parts of Daniel): These are visions full of images. They comfort suffering churches and tell the truth about Jesus’ victory. Do not treat every symbol like a newspaper code.

Meditate. Read slowly. Scripture interprets Scripture. And always read with Christ at the center, because the Spirit who carried the prophets along is the Spirit who glorifies the Son.

## Reflection

Which kind of writing do you usually avoid? What would it look like to read one short passage of that kind this week, patiently?

# The Trinity: one God, three Persons

**Scripture:** Deuteronomy 6:4; Matthew 3:16–17; Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14
**Translation used:** NIV

Christians confess what Scripture teaches, even when it stretches the mind: there is one God, and the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each fully God.

## The passages (NIV)

**Deuteronomy 6:4**
4 Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one.

**Matthew 3:16–17**
16 As soon as Jesus was baptized, he went up out of the water. At that moment heaven was opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and alighting on him. 17 And a voice from heaven said, “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased.”

**Matthew 28:19**
19 Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

**2 Corinthians 13:14**
14 May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

## What this is saying

The Bible does not give a math puzzle. It gives a revelation. God is one. At Jesus’ baptism the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. Disciples are baptized into one name — Father, Son, and Spirit. The church is blessed by all three.

Historic Christian teaching (which Grace Life and evangelical churches share with the wider church) says: there is one God in three Persons; each Person is fully God; the Persons are not three gods, and they are not one Person wearing three masks. We do not have to explain away the mystery. We worship.

This matters for prayer, for the gospel, and for everyday life. The Father sends the Son. The Son accomplishes redemption. The Spirit applies it and lives in you. You are invited into the love that was already there before the world began.

## Reflection

When you pray, do you remember you are speaking to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit? How might that change the way you come to God today?

# The gospel: the good news in full

**Scripture:** 1 Corinthians 15:1–4; Romans 3:21–26; Romans 10:9
**Translation used:** NIV

The gospel is not “try harder” or “be nicer.” It is news. God has done something in Jesus, and you are called to believe it.

## The passages (NIV)

**1 Corinthians 15:1–4**
1 Now, brothers and sisters, I want to remind you of the gospel I preached to you, which you received and on which you have taken your stand. 2 By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you. Otherwise, you have believed in vain. 3 For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, 4 that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.

**Romans 3:23–25**
23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, 24 and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus. 25 God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, through the shedding of his blood—to be received by faith.

**Romans 10:9**
9 If you declare with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

## What this is saying

Paul says this is “of first importance”: Christ died for our sins, he was buried, and he was raised. The gospel names our sin, Christ’s substitution, and his victory over death. Justification is a gift — God declares the ungodly righteous through faith in Jesus, not through works.

Atonement (the LSB and many teachers will also use the word *propitiation*) means Jesus really dealt with the wrath our sin deserved. That is not cruelty. It is mercy: God himself provides the sacrifice.

The right response is repentance and faith — to confess Jesus as Lord and to believe that God raised him. This is the same gospel for a parent, a child, a husband, a wife, a single adult. There is no second way in.

## Reflection

Could you tell this good news, in your own words, to someone in your family this week? Where do you still treat it as something you must add to?

# Law and grace

**Scripture:** Romans 3:19–24; Romans 6:14–15; Galatians 3:24–26; Titus 2:11–12
**Translation used:** NIV

The law is good, and it cannot save you. Grace saves you, and it does not leave you lawless.

## The passages (NIV)

**Romans 3:19–24**
19 Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God. 20 Therefore no one will be declared righteous in God’s sight by the works of the law; rather, through the law we become conscious of our sin. 21 But now apart from the law the righteousness of God has been made known, to which the Law and the Prophets testify. 22 This righteousness is given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no difference between Jew and Gentile, 23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, 24 and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.

**Romans 6:14–15**
14 For sin shall no longer be your master, because you are not under the law, but under grace. 15 What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? By no means!

**Galatians 3:24–26**
24 So the law was our guardian until Christ came that we might be justified by faith. 25 Now that this faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian. 26 So in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith.

**Titus 2:11–12**
11 For the grace of God has appeared that offers salvation to all people. 12 It teaches us to say “No” to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age.

## What this is saying

The law shows us God’s holiness and our sin. It is a guardian, a mirror, a good standard. It is not a ladder into God’s family. Righteousness is given through faith in Jesus.

“Not under the law, but under grace” is not permission to sin. Grace is a teacher. It trains you to say no to ungodliness and yes to a self-controlled life. That includes how you treat a spouse, how you parent, how you handle your body, and how you speak.

If you are exhausted by religious performance, come under grace. If you are using grace as a cover for a habit you will not name, come under the same grace — the kind that teaches and changes you.

# How we got the Bible, and how translations work

**Scripture:** 2 Timothy 3:16–17; Nehemiah 8:8
**Translation used:** NIV

The Bible did not drop from the sky in English last year. God spoke through many writers, in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek. His people have copied, translated, and read those words ever since.

## The passages (NIV)

**2 Timothy 3:16–17**
16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, 17 so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.

**Nehemiah 8:8**
8 They read from the Book of the Law of God, making it clear and giving the meaning so that the people understood what was being read.

## A short history

The Old Testament was written mainly in Hebrew (with some Aramaic). The New Testament was written in Greek. Faithful copyists preserved these texts with extraordinary care. We have a very strong manuscript tradition. When you hear about “variants,” remember that the vast majority are small, and no central doctrine hangs on a doubtful line.

From early on, the church translated the Bible so ordinary people could understand it — into Latin, Syriac, Coptic, and, much later, into English through men like Wycliffe and Tyndale, then the King James Version, and many modern translations.

This study uses three translations Gregory asked us to stay with:

- **NIV** (New International Version): a widely used “thought-for-thought” / mediating translation, clear for reading aloud and for study. The lessons quote the NIV in full.
- **LSB** (Legacy Standard Bible): a more literal translation in the NASB tradition. It often uses “Yahweh” for God’s name and aims at word-level precision. We include LSB notes, not long LSB quotations.
- **NLT** (New Living Translation): a clear, meaning-driven translation that can help a passage open up, especially for newer readers. We may point you there as a second reading, not as a replacement for the NIV text in the lesson.

No translation is itself inspired in the way the original words are. A good translation is a faithful witness. Read one main Bible steadily. Compare a second when a line is hard. And remember Nehemiah 8: the aim is that the people understand.

## Reflection

Which Bible will you actually open this week? If a verse is hard, will you compare a second translation and ask for help rather than giving up?

# End times: what Christians agree on, and where they differ

**Scripture:** John 14:1–3; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–18; Revelation 21:1–5
**Translation used:** NIV

The Bible is clear about the main things, and faithful Christians have not all agreed about the timetable. This lesson aims to be fair and calm, in the mainstream of evangelical teaching.

## The passages (NIV)

**John 14:1–3**
1 “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me. 2 My Father’s house has many rooms; if that were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? 3 And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with me that you also may be where I am.”

**1 Thessalonians 4:16–18**
16 For the Lord himself will come down from heaven, with a loud command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet call of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first. 17 After that, we who are still alive and are left will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will be with the Lord forever. 18 Therefore encourage one another with these words.

**Revelation 21:3–5**
3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Look! God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. 4 ‘He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death’ or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.” 5 He who was seated on the throne said, “I am making everything new!”

## What almost all evangelical Christians agree on

- Jesus will return, personally and visibly.
- The dead will be raised.
- There will be a final judgment.
- God’s people will be with the Lord forever in a renewed creation.
- No one knows the day or the hour; we are called to be ready, holy, and hopeful.

Those are not small points. They are the hope of the church.

## Where faithful readers differ

Christians who love the same Bible differ on how to order some of the details:

- **The millennium** (Revelation 20). *Premillennial* readers expect Christ to return before a future thousand-year reign. *Amillennial* readers see that reign as Christ’s present rule, with a final coming at the end. *Postmillennial* readers expect a future flourishing of the gospel before Christ returns. All three have been held by serious evangelicals.
- **The timing of the “catching up”** in 1 Thessalonians 4 (often called the rapture). Some expect it before a future tribulation, some in the middle, some at Christ’s public return. The text clearly teaches a real gathering to the Lord. The exact placement in a timetable is where the family discussion is.

This app does not require you to pick a chart. It does ask you not to despise brothers and sisters who differ, and not to ignore the clear hope: Jesus is coming, and it will be good for those who are his.

Grace Life and many conservative churches often teach a premillennial hope; other faithful churches do not. Hold your view with an open Bible and a humble heart. Let the point of the texts do their work: “Do not let your hearts be troubled.” “Encourage one another with these words.”

## Reflection

Does the promise of Jesus’ return make you anxious, argumentative, or hopeful? What would it look like to encourage someone in your family with these words this week?

**Scripture:** Ephesians 5:25–33; 1 Peter 3:7; Colossians 3:19
**Translation used:** NIV

If you are a husband, God has given you a clear, heavy, and beautiful work: love your wife as Christ loved the church.

## The passages (NIV)

**Ephesians 5:25–28, 33**
25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her 26 to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, 27 and to present her to himself as a radiant church, without stain or wrinkle or any other blemish, but holy and blameless. 28 In this same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.

33 However, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.

**1 Peter 3:7**
7 Husbands, in the same way be considerate as you live with your wives, and treat them with respect as the weaker partner and as heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers.

**Colossians 3:19**
19 Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them.

## What this is saying

Headship in Ephesians 5 is not a ticket to be served. It is a call to give yourself up. Christ’s love is the pattern: sacrificial, holy, cleansing, nourishing, and faithful. You use your strength for her good, not for your comfort.

Peter says to live with your wife in an understanding way, honoring her as a co-heir of grace. “Weaker partner” is not an insult; it is a call to gentleness, never to control or contempt. If you are harsh, your prayers are hindered. God is not impressed by a man who can lead a meeting and cannot be kind at home.

This is the complementarian pattern taught at Grace Life and by pastors such as John Piper and Tony Evans: equal dignity, distinct callings. Your wife is not your child and not your servant. She is your sister in Christ and your one-flesh partner. Leadership means going first in repentance, in prayer, in provision, in protection, and in the Word.

## How this applies

Ask your wife, or honestly ask yourself: have I been harsh, absent, or selfish? What would giving myself up look like this week — in time, in words, in the work of the house, in spiritual care?

Where is Christlike love asking you to die to yourself for your wife’s good today?

This lesson is adult, frank, and meant to be tasteful. God is not embarrassed by the gift he made. Sex belongs in marriage, and in marriage it is good.

## The passages (NIV)

**Genesis 2:24–25**
24 That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh. 25 Adam and his wife were both naked, and they felt no shame.

**Proverbs 5:15–19**
15 Drink water from your own cistern, running water from your own well. 16 Should your springs overflow in the streets, your streams of water in the public squares? 17 Let them be yours alone, never to be shared with strangers. 18 May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth. 19 A loving doe, a graceful deer—may her breasts satisfy you always, may you ever be intoxicated with her love.

**1 Corinthians 7:3–5**
3 The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. 4 The wife does not have authority over her own body but yields it to her husband. **Hebrews 13:4**
4 Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the adulterer and all the sexually immoral.

## What this is saying

One flesh is more than a ceremony. God designed sexual intimacy as a joining of husband and wife — loyal, embodied, joyful, and without shame. Proverbs 5 is not prudish. It tells a husband to delight in his wife, and only in his wife.

1 Corinthians 7 is strikingly mutual. Authority over the body is yielded both ways. Sex is not a husband’s demand, and it is not a wife’s bargaining chip. It is a gift you give to one another. Depriving one another, except by brief mutual agreement for prayer, opens a door to temptation.

Purity in marriage still matters. Pornography is not a private harmless habit. It trains you to take, to compare, and to hide. It is unfaithfulness of the heart, and often of the body, and it wounds your wife even when she does not know. Adultery, fantasy you feed, and sexual hardness or pressure are all out of place in a marriage bed that is to be kept honorable.

Be a generous, gentle, unselfish husband. Talk honestly with your wife. If there is pain, history, or a stuck pattern, get wise help rather than staying in silence or in sin. Desire for your wife is not dirty. Using her, neglecting her, or replacing her with a screen is.

Have you treated intimacy as a right to take, a subject to avoid, or a gift to give? What would honorable, joyful faithfulness look like with your wife this season?

3 The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. 4 The wife does not have authority over her own body but yields it to her husband. In the same way, the husband does not have authority over his own body but yields it to his wife. 5 Do not deprive each other except perhaps by mutual consent and for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again so that Satan will not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

**Hebrews 13:4**
4 Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the adulterer and all the sexually immoral.

## What this is saying

One flesh is a shared gift. The Song of Songs is not ashamed of desire inside a faithful bond: “My beloved is mine and I am his.” God does not only tolerate a wife’s pleasure; he designed mutual joy.

1 Corinthians 7 is careful and mutual. This is not a license for a husband to demand, and it is not a license for a wife to use sex as a reward or a punishment. You yield to one another. There may be wise, agreed seasons of waiting for prayer, or for real reasons of health and weariness. Then you come together again, kindly, so that temptation does not get a foothold.

The marriage bed is to be kept pure. That means loyalty in body and in mind. Pornography, romantic comparison, hidden chats, or sexual involvement outside the marriage all break covenant. If you have been hurt, or if intimacy has become a place of fear, pressure, or emptiness, you are not required to pretend. Tell the truth to God, and, as it is safe, to your husband or to a wise counselor. Healing and holiness can grow together.

A wife’s part is not reluctant endurance only. It is generous, honest, and chaste love — the kind that does her husband good and also tells the truth about her own heart and body.

## Reflection

Have you treated intimacy as a duty to survive, a tool to manage, or a gift to give and receive? What would honorable, joyful faithfulness look like with your husband this season?
